name: Five scenario presets and domain terminology

labels: Your flu test is positive. What’s the chance you really have flu? That’s precision—and it also depends on how common flu is among the people tested.Compare 10% and 50% sick using the same test. Precision changes, even though the portion of sick people correctly testing positive (TPR) and the portion of people without flu getting a false alarm (FPR) stay the same.

Your car’s sensor slams the emergency brakes! Is there really an obstacle ahead? In autonomous emergency braking (AEB), safety demands high sensitivity (TPR), but phantom braking (FP) risks rear-end crashes.Compare how obstacle frequency and sensor confidence trade off crash avoidance against phantom stops.

An email was sent to your Spam folder. Is it really junk—or an important email? That’s precision. In spam filtering, a false alarm (good email discarded) is far worse than junk reaching your Inbox.Notice how spam rate in incoming email shifts precision, even with a fixed classification model.

Your card was declined for suspicious activity. Is it a real thief or a false alarm? Credit card fraud is rare (~1–2%), so even an accurate detector produces false alarms due to the base-rate fallacy.See why high sensitivity causes frequent card blocks when fraud is rare.

The model predicts positive. How likely is the actual class to be positive? That’s precision—and it also depends on class prevalence (the positive portion).Compare 10% and 50% positives with the same model and threshold. Precision changes, while the true positive rate (TPR, or recall) and false positive rate (FPR) stay the same.
